titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Embassy in Paraguay to the Department of State

div.head: 404. Telegram From the Embassy in Paraguay to the Department of State
div.p: 5204. Subject: (C) Ambassador’s August 29 meeting with President Stroessner: “ABC Color.”

2. Summary: The Ambassador discussed the closure of “ABC Color” with President Stroessner on August 29. In exchanges that went on for an hour, the President repeatedly insisted that he did not want to talk about the “ABC” issue, while the Ambassador described the widespread U.S. concern over the matter and cautioned him about the continued problem it would pose for our bilateral relations. Out of the blue, Stroessner renewed his earlier requests for C–130 and F–5 aircraft for his air force. The Ambassador responded that this was precisely the kind of thing the U.S. could not do while “ABC” remained closed. Stroessner concluded by saying that he considered the matter to be a “dead issue.” End summary.

3. The Ambassador called on President Stroessner August 29 to discuss the problem of the continued closure of “ABC Color.” The Ambassador opened the discussion by describing his recent consultations in Washington, stressing the concern throughout the USG over the matter. He noted that this concern crossed party and ideological lines in the Congress, as indicated by the recent resolution on the subject.

4. President Stroessner interjected at this point that as far as he was concerned the “ABC” issue was something he did not want to talk about anymore. The Ambassador responded that it was important for the GOP to understand that the continued closure of “ABC” would mean continued problems in our bilateral relations. It would prevent the U.S. from deepening cooperation with Paraguay in matters affecting our mutual interests. Would the President give him a definitive answer on “ABC’s” future?

5. Sliding away from a direct response, Stroessner
reiterated his desire not to pursue the discussion. He said the closure of “ABC” had been necessary, adding that for the sake of the Paraguayan people he could not afford to relax his grip. He pointed to Peru and Argentina as examples of what happened when there was “democracy without firmness.” He went on to recite a somewhat colored version of Paraguay’s chaotic political history during the first half of the 20th century, up until his accession to power. This could not be allowed to recur. He repeated that he did not wish to discuss the subject further.

6. The Ambassador asked if the GOP had any flexibility on the “ABC” issue. Perhaps “ABC” owner Zuccolillo might be willing to discuss conditions under which the paper could re-open. The President dismissed this possibility, leaving no doubt that he was not willing to treat with Zuccolillo. He added that U.S. complaints over the “ABC” matter were interference in Paraguay’s internal affairs, and said he was particularly stung by the Embassy’s public protest over the paper’s closure in March. No other country, he said, had raised the matter with him. Even the UK Deputy Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs, who called on him earlier this month, had agreed that it was an internal matter and had accepted the fact that the “ABC” question was now closed.

7. At this point, the President said there was something he wanted to raise. Paraguay, which had supported the U.S. faithfully over the years, needed U.S. help. He said the U.S. had promised to provide a C–130 aircraft to the Paraguayan Air Force back in 1971. He was still waiting. In addition, he said, his air force needed some F–5 aircraft, provision of which should cause the U.S. no difficulty since they were purely defensive. Defense Minister Martinez would be in touch with the Ambassador shortly to provide details.

8. The Ambassador said he hadn’t wanted to seem to be threatening but was surprised at this request, and at the apparent unwillingness of the GOP to listen to what he had been repeating over the past two years about how human rights issues affected our ability to provide military equipment. He said there was no prospect that the U.S. would be willing to sell such equipment to Paraguay as long as “ABC” was closed. Moreover, the closure placed even our modest IMET program in serious jeopardy in the Congress. This was exactly what he meant when he said that continued closure of “ABC” would limit possibilities for mutual cooperation.

9. The Ambassador added that as he had told Foreign Minister Saldivar, a meeting between Saldivar and the
Secretary during Saldivar’s forthcoming trip to the U.S. would not be possible. The Embassy would, however, seek to arrange a meeting with Assistant Secretary Motley. The President said that this would be fine.

10. At this point, the conversation turned to other matters (which will be reported in separate messages). As the Ambassador was leaving, however, the President reminded him of his desire for F–5s and commented philosophically that he remained in office not because he liked the job, but to protect his people against the kind of political upheavals which had convulsed Paraguay so often in the 20th century.

11. The President was calm and relaxed throughout the meeting, though he clearly did not relish the persistent discussion of “ABC.” We take his comments to be a definitive “no” to any re-opening of “ABC”. Our views on the U.S. response to this position will be the subject of a separate message.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840554–0030. Secret; Immediate.

In telegram 5144 from Asuncion, August 28, the Embassy reported on Davis’ August 27 meeting with Saldívar writing: “The Ambassador discussed the ‘ABC Color’ closure with the Foreign Minister August 27, emphasizing the widespread concern over the case throughout the USG. The Foreign Minister argued for a meeting with the Secretary to present Paraguay’s side of the case, but avoided saying anything definitive about the paper’s future.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840547–0813)

House Congressional Resolution 331 passed on June 29 and was approved by the Senate on July 27, stating, in part: “Concurrent resolution to condemn the closing of ABC Color, the only independent newspaper in Paraguay, and to urge the Government of Paraguay to permit the reopening of that newspaper and to guarantee freedom of the press.”
No memorandum of conversation of has been found.

In telegram 5227 from Asuncion, August 30, the Embassy reported that during his August 29 meeting with Davis, Stroessner had discussed his possible travel plans. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840555–0328) In telegram 5229 from Asuncion, August 30, the Embassy reported on developments in the Colorado Party, noting that during Davis’ August 29 meeting, Stroessner described “the open competition within the party as an example of democracy in action.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840555–0353)

In telegram 5531 from Asuncion, September 14, the Embassy wrote: “The Embassy believes there is little or no chance of persuading President Stroessner to permit the reopening of ‘ABC Color.’ To underline our concern and disapproval, we should therefore distance ourselves from the Stroessner government. To do this, we should carefully monitor the activities of all U.S. agencies to reduce our profile and cut back on those that suggest too close identification with the government.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840587–0282)
